title: Recall the horizontal assymptotes of arctan
text: Start with the horizontal asymptotes of $$\arctan(x), $$ which are $$y=\frac{-\pi}{2}$$ and $$y=\frac{\pi}{2}$$.\n##figure1.gif##

figureAlts.figure1.gif: Graph of the inverse trigonometric function theta equals arctangent of x. The horizontal axis is x, and the vertical axis is theta. The curve is strictly increasing for all real numbers, passing through the origin. It approaches, but never touches, two horizontal dashed lines representing asymptotes at theta equals pi over two, and theta equals negative pi over two.

title: Transform the asymptotes
text: Apply the transformations to these $$y-$$ values: first multiply by the vertical scale (3), then add the vertical shift ( $$\pi$$ ).\n##figure2.gif##

figureAlts.figure2.gif: Graph showing three related inverse trigonometric curves on a coordinate plane with a horizontal x-axis and a vertical theta-axis. The first curve, drawn as a dashed line, is theta equals arctangent of x, bounded between horizontal asymptotes at pi over two and negative pi over 2. The second curve, drawn as a dotted line, is theta equals three times arctangent of x; representing a vertical stretch. It is bounded between horizontal asymptotes at theta values three pi over 2 and negative three pi over two. The third curve, drawn as a solid line, is theta equals three times arctangent of x plus pi; representing an upward vertical shift. This final solid curve is strictly increasing and approaches two horizontal dashed-line asymptotes: an upper asymptote at theta equals five pi over two, and a lower asymptote at theta equals negative pi over two.
